note: The answer correctly attributes the variability to the bailed/decanted method cites the atmosphere-exposure reason and notes the DO/Eh/temperature restriction with qualified reporting but omits the required-vs-recommended in-situ distinction the anoxic/reducing inert-gas restriction and the suction-lift pump warning; no 'must not' item is violated. Unmet: States ORP DO and temperature are required in situ where possible while pH conductivity and turbidity are only recommended; States that in anoxic or reducing groundwater subsample procedures must not be used at all unless handled under an inert gas; Warns a peristaltic or other suction-lift pump must not be used for ORP or DO because negative pressure volatilises dissolved gases

The answer makes the bracketing/1.68-buffer points but omits the pH 1.68–10 accuracy range the ±10 °C buffer-temperature requirement and the ±0.05 pH unit buffer check and it does not violate any must-not item. Unmet: Standard pH procedure expected accurate over roughly pH 1.68 to 10; Calibration buffers must be within about 10 C of sample temperature; Check of buffer nearest sample pH should be within about 0.05 pH unit or recalibrate

The answer correctly states the low-pH compensation problem and the 50 percent figure but omits the transport-property cause the largest-source-of-error statement the 25 °C equilibration check its pass bar and the comment-field reporting requirement. Unmet: Explains the cause as the hydrogen ion having different transport properties from other ions and contributing a large share of the conductance at low pH; States that at low pH the temperature correction can be the single largest source of error; Describes the check of comparing the in-situ reading against the same water equilibrated to 25 C; Gives the pass bar for that check as within about 5 microsiemens per centimetre at or below 100 or about 3 percent above that; States that if an alternative low-pH compensation method is used the compensation factor has to be recorded in the comment field

The answer correctly covers the subsample qualifier/comment rule (including temperature DO Eh) the ban on sampling flow-cell discharge and cites the sources but omits the storage limits and the on-site/in-situ time-sensitivity point. Unmet: Storage limits: clean amber bottle out of sunlight chilled at or below 4 C no longer than 24 hours; Turbidity is time sensitive and should be measured on site preferably in situ

The answer makes the temperature-during-transport point and avoids the prohibited assertions but omits condensation the other bench biases the in-situ preference and the equilibration/warming caveat. Unmet: Identifies condensation on the sample cell as a plausible source of bias when sample water is much colder than air without establishing it as the actual cause; Names the other bench-measurement biases: cell orientation coloured water gas bubbles scratched or dirty sample cells; Explains the preference for in-situ or pumped dynamic measurement while requiring checks of both methods before deciding which reading is reliable; Notes that letting the sample equilibrate to ambient temperature reduces condensation but warming the sample can change particle associations in the water

The answer covers the airtight flow-through cell and the temperature/pH/electrode logging but omits the drift/thermal-equilibrium timing the 15-20 minute then 10-minute reading schedule the slower/asymmetric ORP response and the nearest-10-mV reporting rule. Unmet: states the tubing must be relatively impermeable to oxygen the fittings airtight and atmospheric oxygen purged from the tubing and flow channels before measuring; states the reading drifts until thermal equilibrium is reached and that this can take longer than 30 minutes; After thermal equilibration takes readings every few minutes for 15-20 minutes and then about every 10 minutes until at least 30 minutes from the initial measurement and a constant potential.; notes the ORP system responds more slowly than pH and asymmetrically taking longer in one direction than the other; States calculated Eh is reported to the nearest 10 mV.

The answer correctly covers barometric pressure at 1 mm Hg from a checked barometer and links salinity correction to specific conductance but omits the 100%-saturation goal 0.1 C temperature precision the computed-from-signal/ionic-strength point droplet checks the USGS post-measurement salinity preference and the recalibration-per-salinity-change note. Unmet: Goal of one-point calibration is a 100% oxygen-saturated environment with DO sensor and its temperature sensor at the same temperature; Temperature read to the nearest 0.1 C; Reported concentration computed from sensor signal with temperature and ionic strength; sensor not measuring mg/L directly; Checks for droplets on optical module and temperature sensor recalibrates if present; does not assume unidentified probe is optical; USGS prefers applying manual salinity correction after calibration and measurement; distinguishes automatic conductivity-based compensation; Notes manual salinity correction at calibration forces recalibration for each change in field salinity

The answer states the EPA before-use calibration requirement and the end-of-day check but omits the sampling-location exemption the midday-drift qualification rule the pre-deployment/recovery sonde check the DO post-calibration check details and the QA-plan fallback for drift criteria. Unmet: EPA cadence includes an end-of-day calibration check except when calibrated at each sampling location under the stated exemption; Midday drift check: recalibrate before treating later data as unaffected; preceding data qualified; Continuously deployed sonde calibrated before deployment and checked on recovery; DO post-calibration check in measurement mode recording DO temperature and barometric pressure against an oxygen-solubility chart; SOP's own drift criteria apply only when the project QA plan does not specify its own

The answer gives the ±0.2 °C accuracy requirement and the certified/traceable verification but omits the contrast with pH/conductivity adjustment and never mentions the faulty-thermistor effect on specific conductance. Unmet: States that checking a temperature sensor means verifying its accuracy across the range of use not adjusting it to a standard the way a pH or conductivity sensor is adjusted; States that a faulty or drifting thermistor in the conductivity cell produces wrong specific conductance values

The answer gives the 0.5-3%/°C range the 0.019-0.020 linear factor the t-minus-25 correction and the compensated-display idea but omits that the corrected value is specific conductance to be reported/trended and omits the ±5 percent accuracy for 5-35 °C and pH 4-11. Unmet: States the corrected value is specific conductance referenced to 25 C which is what should be reported and trended; States temperature compensation is typically accurate to ±5 percent for 5-35 °C and pH 4-11

The answer correctly states the two tables agree and do not conflict but omits the cross-reference to the multiparameter chapter the note that accuracy varies by model/manufacturer and the persistent-variability procedure. Unmet: states the general field-measurement chapter itself points multiparameter users to the multiparameter chapter for criteria of the same kind; states the criteria are standard sensor stabilisation criteria and that actual sensor accuracy varies by model and manufacturer which is a separate matter; For persistent variability extends equilibration and records additional measurements then either reports the median of the final five or more readings or selects a representative final reading using site knowledge and professional judgment documenting the decision

The answer makes most points (ZoBell check temperature-dependent table value 15–30 min equilibration ±5 mV pass window 90-day chilled stability) but omits the 430 mV value at 25 °C and the interpolation of between-row temperatures and it carries no source citations. Unmet: Gives the theoretical ZoBell Eh at 25 C as about 430 mV; States values for temperatures between table rows are interpolated

The answer gives all six per-parameter stabilization criteria the five-or-more-readings basis and the 60-second minimum wait but omits that some instruments need longer per the manufacturer up to several minutes depending on the temperature step. Unmet: 60 seconds is a minimum and some instruments need longer per manufacturer up to several minutes depending on temperature step

The answer makes most points (low ionic strength cause circuit explanation alternate electrode KCl fix at ~150 µS/cm <0.01 pH effect no-stir warning) but omits the ionic-strength/liquid-junction causes and the condition that KCl is used only after the normal procedure fails to stabilise. Unmet: Names large ionic-strength difference between sample and buffers and enlarged liquid-junction potential as contributing causes; States KCl procedure used only after normal procedure tried and reading would not stabilise

The answer states both A6.8 criteria (±0.1 pH unit ±0.3 below 75 µS/cm) and contrasts them with A6.4's 0.05 pH-unit final-buffer check without replacing the check inventing a threshold or confusing calibration with stabilisation.

The answer correctly gives the ±0.2 mg/L optical-DO criterion says 0.3 mg/L exceeds it and cites the median-of-final-three rule but it omits the longer-equilibration/median-of-five-or-representative-reading path and never notes that ORP is not covered by the DO stabilisation table. Unmet: Allows longer equilibration and additional readings then either the median of the final five or more readings or a representative final reading selected using site knowledge and professional judgment with the decision documented; Notes that ORP is not covered by that stabilisation table and is instead judged by the potential holding constant over the reading sequence

The answer correctly says order matters puts temperature first and specific conductance before pH and gives the low-to-high ionic-strength rationale but omits the ion-selective/fluorescence sensors and the DO-last exception the conductivity-before-pH contamination reason the three DIW rinses and the before-each-field-use check. Unmet: Gives general remaining order as pH DO ORP turbidity then ion-selective and fluorescence sensors while allowing A6.2's two-point DO calibration exception requiring DO last to avoid sodium-sulfite interference; States specifically that conductivity must be calibrated before pH because pH buffers and electrode filling solutions are high in ionic strength and are a contamination source; States the sensors are rinsed three times with deionized water between different standards; States the sonde is calibrated or checked before each field use

The answer correctly names pH DO specific conductance and ORP as temperature-dependent channels but it never explains the specific temperature dependence for specific conductance dissolved oxygen or pH buffers nor notes the separate temperature-sensor location on a multiparameter instrument. Unmet: Explains for specific conductance that the reported value is a temperature-corrected number computed from the measured temperature; Explains for dissolved oxygen that the reported concentration is computed from the sensor signal together with temperature; Explains for pH that the buffer values used to calibrate it depend on temperature; Notes that on a multiparameter instrument the temperature sensor typically sits in a different part of the instrument from the pH electrode

The answer correctly places pH downstream of conductivity but omits the cell-design caveat the keep-close/shield-from-sunlight guidance and the design-dependent probe positioning; it also adds an unsupported contamination rationale though it does not repeat the calibration order or recommend a turbidity sample from the discharge. Unmet: States the flow cell should be kept as close to the source water as possible and shielded from direct sunlight; Notes the specific-conductance probe position relative to the pH electrode depends on the flow-cell design

The answer correctly says the temperature sensor is verified rather than calibrated names a NIST-traceable thermometer and gives an annual cadence but omits the ±0.2 C accuracy specification and the calibration-solution/evaporation point. Unmet: Gives required accuracy as about ±0.2 C where the sensor is bundled on a multiparameter instrument and used to correct another parameter; States calibration solution must cover probe and temperature sensor; identifies evaporation of moisture as a DO air-calibration concern

The answer correctly notes the USGS table stops at 40 °C and reaches down to 600 mm Hg but misstates the EPA chart's temperature (says 40 °C not 45 °C) and pressure floor (says 730 mm Hg not ~690 mm Hg) and omits the simultaneous-bound explanation generated-value source and salinity correction factors. Unmet: EPA chart's temperature coverage runs to 45 C and gives no value above that; EPA chart bottoms out around 690 mmHg; Explains different table bounds and that neither printed table covers simultaneous temperature above 40 °C and pressure below 690 mmHg; supported generated values require a separate source; Notes only the USGS chapter supplies salinity correction factors which the EPA chart does not carry

The answer withholds both table values the 0.03 mg/L difference the Benson and Krause basis and the ±0.2 mg/L tolerance comparison and instead picks the EPA table unconditionally rather than advising use of the table matching the governing protocol. Unmet: gives the USGS table value at 20.0 C and 760 mmHg as about 9.09 mg/L; gives the EPA chart value at 20 C and 760 mmHg as about 9.06 mg/L; states the difference is 0.03 mg/L and assesses its significance against the applicable procedure; notes the USGS values are generated from the Benson and Krause equations; compares the 0.03 mg/L difference with the USGS saturation-check tolerance of ±0.2 mg/L; advises using the table belonging to whichever protocol the work is being done under consistently rather than mixing them

The answer states the DO must be multiplied by the salinity correction factor gives 0.8235 for 20 °C at 50 000 µS/cm and attributes it to USGS Table 6.2-4 with no invented factor and no addition/division.

The answer states the 2 000 µS/cm saline-water threshold but never asks for the upstream pods' specific conductance and gives no 1.0000 zero-conductance factor so only part of the first point is made; no 'must not' item is violated. Unmet: Explains the manual's saline-water correction applies above 2 000 µS/cm and asks for the upstream specific conductance before deciding; freshwater does not imply zero conductivity; Gives 1.0000 at zero specific conductance without extending that exact factor to all freshwater

The answer correctly covers the 25 C specific-conductance basis the need to temperature-correct raw readings automatic meter compensation and checking the pod's output but omits the A6.2 >2 000 µS/cm saline-water definition and its instrument/calibration/salt dependence. Unmet: Notes A6.2 defines saline waters as specific conductance greater than 2 000 microsiemens per centimetre where the correction varies with instrument type calibration method and salts in solution

The answer gives the two table values and the ~1.0 mg/L drop but it applies the freshwater solubility unchanged to the brackish site (violating a must-not) and it omits the pressure dependence the salinity correction and the caveat that the site-specific split cannot be established from these readings alone. Unmet: states equilibrium saturation also depends on barometric pressure so the site's actual pressure changes the benchmark; states that in brackish water the freshwater value must be reduced by a salinity correction factor before comparison; states the actual warming contribution and remaining drop cannot be established from these readings alone (pressure salinity initial saturation not given)
All three must-contain points are stated (60-second equilibration median of values within ~60 seconds at each vertical and median of the final three or more readings) and no must-not item appears.

The answer approves diluting a commercial standard generally and omits the no-dilution rule and the suspension-matrix/nonlinearity explanation violating the 'must not' item against approving dilution of commercial standards other than 4 000-unit formazin. Unmet: states that commercial calibration solutions must not be diluted; gives 4 000-unit formazin as the one exception that may be diluted; explains that diluting changes the suspension matrix so the dilutions are no longer linear

Four of five must-contain points are made correctly but the answer omits that a small well-mixed stream under about 5 feet wide can be represented by a single centroid point (it instead gives the narrower-stream EWI increment rule). Unmet: Small well-mixed stream under about 5 feet wide can be represented by a single centroid point

The answer correctly states flocculated calibrants must not be used but it assumes all settled calibrant must be discarded without checking whether the settled layer is reversible settling versus flocculation. Unmet: Requires checking whether the settled layer is reversible settling or flocculation along with labeled expiry and storage compliance; rejects flocculated expired or compromised calibrant rather than assuming all settled calibrant must be discarded
The answer gives the correct 9.09 mg/L value for 20 °C at 760 mmHg attributes it to the USGS table and identifies it as freshwater with no invented value or datasheet use.

The answer gives the <0.5 mg/L expectation and the above-0.5/negative remediation steps but omits that the 0.5 mg/L value may be adjusted to the project's or instrument's accuracy requirements. Unmet: Notes the 0.5 mg/L value assumes an instrument accuracy of about ±0.2 mg/L and may be adjusted to the project's or instrument's accuracy requirements

Both values are drawn from the same USGS table and the direction of change is correct but the 35 °C value is misread as 6.90 mg/L instead of 6.95 mg/L so the stated decrease of 2.19 mg/L is also wrong rather than 2.14 mg/L. Unmet: Gives 6.95 mg/L for 35.0 °C at 760 mmHg; States equilibrium saturation decreases by 2.14 mg/L about 2 mg/L

The answer gives the <3 µS/cm guideline and says 6 µS/cm exceeds it but never explains that this is the meter's low-end zero-response check made with the dry cell in air or DIW. Unmet: Explains this is the meter's low-end zero-response check made with the dry cell in air or in deionized water

The answer correctly gives the saturated-air setup the 10–15 minute saturation/warm-up and the chart comparison with ±0.2 mg/L and repeat but omits that the temperature sensor must not touch the wet material and omits the weather-service/elevation caveat for barometric pressure. Unmet: Neither the probe nor the temperature sensor may touch the wet sponge or towel; Barometric pressure must come from an on-site barometer not a weather service unless corrected for elevation

The answer correctly rules out DIW for calibration selects the bracketing 500 µS/cm standard and separates the zero-response check from calibration but it omits the reason that sub-200 µS/cm standards are easily biased by dilution or contamination. Unmet: States calibration standards greater than 200 µS/cm are recommended because lower ones are easily biased by dilution or contamination

The answer gives the 60-second minimum its thermal-equilibrium purpose and the longer-equilibration/manufacturer caveat but never notes that equilibration can run from 60 seconds to several minutes depending on the temperature difference. Unmet: Notes equilibration can run from 60 seconds to several minutes depending on the temperature difference

The answer gives the temperature DO and pH stabilization tolerances but omits the specific-conductance and turbidity criteria and never states the five-or-more-consecutive-readings basis so it is only partially complete. Unmet: States specific conductance must be within ±5 µS/cm at or below 100 µS/cm and ±3 percent above 100 µS/cm; Gives turbidity stabilization as ±0.5 TU or ±5 percent whichever is greater at or below 100 TU; above 100 TU uses ±10 percent; Assesses stabilization over about five or more consecutive readings

The answer states the two-point minimum and gives the valid 6 °C/10 °C example but omits the ±2 °C extrema rule the ±4 °C mean rule and the at-most-five-points note and cites no sources. Unmet: States the points must be within ±2 °C of the annual minimum and maximum; States the points must be within ±4 °C of the annual mean; Notes this range-verification procedure requires at most five points without generalizing to every certification procedure

The answer states both methods are acceptable and describes the in situ site-visit route but omits the 12-month requirement and the pre-field-trip one-point check and gives no citations. Unmet: States verification is required at least once every 12 months; States a one-point check against a certified sensor is also required immediately before a field trip

Three of four must-contain points are made correctly but the answer never gives 430 mV as the theoretical Eh of ZoBell's at 25 °C and no must-not item is violated. Unmet: Gives 430 mV as the theoretical Eh of ZoBell's at 25 °C

The answer correctly gives both EPA-rounded values (0.40 and 65) but only mentions the EPA 180.1 drinking-water exception without stating the USGS/ASTM default rule or the GLI Method 2 and ISO 7027 alternatives. Unmet: Notes USGS follows ASTM guidelines unless the data were collected for drinking-water compliance under EPA 180.1 GLI Method 2 or ISO 7027

The answer asserts Eh is simply another name for the probe's ORP output and that the millivolt reading is the same numerical value as Eh violating the 'must not' item on interchangeability and it omits the noble-metal/equilibrium definition the reference-electrode caveat and the Eref addition step. Unmet: states that Eh is an equilibrium potential developed at the boundary between a noble-metal electrode and the water and reflects the redox-active species in solution; states that the millivolts the probe reads are not Eh on their own because that raw reading is against the probe's own reference electrode; states that getting Eh means adding the reference electrode's own potential to the measured reading
All three must-contain points are made correctly no must-not item is violated and both required sources are cited.

The answer correctly states that a required-step departure must be documented and independently quality assured and that a log note alone is insufficient but it never says the same expectation applies to departures from recommended procedures. Unmet: The same documentation-plus-independent-QA expectation applies to departures from recommended procedures

All three must-contain points are made but the answer invents a stabilization duration ('the stabilization step is usually only a few minutes') that no excerpt gives violating the 'invents a waiting time' must-not.

The answer correctly identifies TU as turbidity units a generic label for instruments of undefined design and notes the instrument type is not conveyed but it omits the historical JTU/FTU labels warning; no must-not items are violated. Unmet: warns that older data can also carry historical labels - Jackson turbidity units (JTU) or formazin turbidity units (FTU) - which are no longer in normal use
All three must-contain points are made correctly and no must-not item is violated.

The answer correctly defines specific conductance as the conductance of 1 cm³ at 25 °C but omits the resistance/siemens relationship the cell-constant normalization and the caveat that µS/cm alone does not establish temperature compensation. Unmet: Raw conductance is the inverse of resistance measured in siemens; Conductivity equals conductance times the cell constant (spacing/area) a geometry-normalized property; Distinguishes conductivity from specific conductance at 25 °C; µS/cm alone does not establish temperature compensation so the reference temperature must be checked

The answer correctly contrasts required policy with multiple acceptable recommended alternatives but it never states that the reason for the selection among recommended options must be documented so one must-contain point is missed. Unmet: states that when a recommended step is involved the reason for picking the option you picked has to be written down

The answer correctly states no conversion is needed since mho and siemens are the same unit but omits the 1971 changeover the interchangeable terminology and the temperature-reference caveat. Unmet: Mhos were the normal reporting unit for older data changeover around 1971; Specific conductance specific electrical conductance and electrical conductivity all used for the same measurement; Because conductivity is not always referenced to a standard temperature the measurement/reference temperature must be reported and checked against older values

The answer correctly presents both immersion options with a sonde-configuration restriction but omits that calibration occurs in a separate vessel of standard rather than the monitored water and omits the whole-head trade-off of larger standard volume and contamination/dilution risk. Unmet: States either way the calibration is done in a separate vessel with the sensor sitting in the calibration standard not in the water body being monitored; Gives the trade-off for putting the whole head in: it takes a lot more standard and brings a risk of contaminating or diluting that standard

The answer correctly states the isolation and bubble-free-surface difficulties of sensor-only immersion but omits the rinsing steps and the steady-stand step and adds no invented values or universal no-disadvantage claim. Unmet: Notes the practical steps: rinsing with deionized water then the standard and working bubbles off by agitating the sonde or running the wiper before the reading; Notes the sonde is then set steady — stood vertically on a flat surface or held in a stand — rather than hand-held
All four must-contain points are stated (detergent first then 5% HCl manufacturer guidance check and the nitric acid/aqua regia warning for platinum electrodes) and no must-not item appears.

The answer warns that replacing the cable may require recertification and it does not call the swap a simple no-follow-up fix invent any interval/cost/provider or confuse recertification with routine calibration.

The answer gives the erratic-reading checks (connections cable break weak batteries) but never distinguishes them from the dirty-sensor and expired-verification causes of inaccurate readings so one must-contain point is missed. Unmet: Distinguishes the erratic-reading checks from dirty-sensor and expired-verification causes of inaccurate readings noting weak batteries can cause either

The answer correctly says the label follows the instrument's optical design and expands NTU/FNU but it only maps NTU to broadband and FNU to near-infrared rather than the full designation lists and it names only 90° and backscatter (misattributing 180° to backscatter) without covering attenuation ratio and multibeam labels; no must-not item is violated. Unmet: Broad-spectrum 400-680 nm corresponds to NTU NTRU BU AU NTMU; FNU FNRU FBU FAU FNMU to 780-900 nm near-infrared; Detector arrangement sets the other half: 90° nephelometry gives plain nephelometric labels; backscatter attenuation ratio and multibeam each have distinct labels
The answer gives the 2-hour maximum soak the thorough deionized-water rinse afterwards and upholds that the manufacturer's specific cleaning instructions govern with no must-not violation.
The answer makes all four required points and avoids the prohibited claims citing the USGS turbidity document.

The answer correctly says not to shake and to invert about 25 times at roughly one second per inversion but it omits letting bubbles clear before filling the cell and omits the guidance about avoiding pouring straight from the bottle and pouring off immediately after mixing. Unmet: says to let the bubbles clear before filling the measurement cell; notes that reading straight from the bottle into the cell is best avoided and that if it cannot be avoided the sample is poured off immediately after mixing so the particles do not settle out

The answer declines to endorse 1.0 mg/L as the pod's alarm and says the configured threshold is unavailable but it omits the spectrophotometric verification trigger and the Rhodazine D range point entirely. Unmet: States that anticipated DO below 1.0 mg/L triggers instrument-specific spectrophotometric verification for optical sensors before reporting not an alarm at or below 1.0 mg/L; Notes that the Rhodazine D spectrophotometric method covers roughly 0.025 to 1.0 mg/L underscoring the figure is about verifying the instrument not judging the water

The answer correctly declines and notes the pod's threshold is unavailable but it omits the chapter's river-water and groundwater descriptions and never distinguishes a documented range from a configured alarm limit. Unmet: States 6.5–8.5 is the chapter's description of uncontaminated river water not a recommended configuration limit; States most groundwaters in the US run 6.0–8.5 so one freshwater figure may not fit both site types; Distinguishes the range the chapter describes from a limit configured for the pod

The answer does say the pod's threshold is unavailable but it presents the 1.0 mg/L figure as a general ecological hypoxic limit and applies it to the reading violating the must-not against treating that figure as an ecological limit and it never ties the figure to the chapter's optical-sensor verification requirement. Unmet: Attributes the below-1.0 mg/L hypoxic-to-anoxic wording to the USGS optical-sensor verification discussion not a universal ecological definition; States the 1.0 mg/L figure is where the chapter requires an optical sensor's low-range accuracy to be independently documented before reporting not an ecological limit for the pod

The answer correctly states the electrode must never go in the stock bottle that buffer is poured into a separate container and that used solution is discarded but it omits the recommendation to decant into a labelled dedicated secondary bottle for field use. Unmet: Recommends decanting into a dedicated secondary bottle for field use labelled with value lot number and expiration date

The answer correctly declines to adopt 19 NTU and notes the pod's threshold is unavailable but it omits the chapter's reported groundwater turbidity figures the observation-vs-recommendation distinction and the qualitative nature of turbidity. Unmet: States chapter reports natural groundwater turbidity up to 19 units and contaminated groundwater can run higher attributed to chapter; States chapter's groundwater figures describe observations not a recommended flagging value; Reiterates turbidity is a relative qualitative indicator not a numeric pass/fail band

The answer is a refusal that withholds the requested guidance and makes none of the must-contain points though it avoids the must-not items. Unmet: States that the decanted field bottles should be refreshed before every field trip; States that solution past its expiration date must not be used; States that the solutions must be protected from wide temperature swings and from extreme heat or freezing; States that solution which has been frozen or overheated can no longer be assumed valid and should be discarded; Notes that the lot number expiration date and the temperature at use are recorded in the instrument logbook

The answer declines to judge the reading cites the chapter's groundwater description as reference and notes the pod threshold is unavailable but it never states that turbidity is a relative uncalibrated index not judged against a numeric range. Unmet: States turbidity is treated as a relative uncalibrated index here and is not judged against a numeric range

Five of six must-contain points are made correctly (goal chamber wetting loose screw-on chamber 5–10 min equilibration pressure to nearest mm Hg) and no must-not is violated but the answer never states that barometric pressure must be measured at the calibration altitude rather than corrected from elsewhere. Unmet: Barometric pressure measured at the altitude where calibration is done not corrected from elsewhere

The answer gives the ±0.2 mg/L/2 percent verification the calibrated conductivity sensor for brackish water and applying correction after calibration but omits the water-droplet check/recalibration and the warning that manual salinity entry during calibration forces recalibration for each field salinity change. Unmet: Checks optical module and temperature-sensor surfaces and repeats calibration if water droplets were present; Notes manual salinity correction during calibration forces recalibration for every field salinity change

The answer correctly brackets the ~700 µS/cm sample with 500 and 1 413 µS/cm standards recommends standards above 200 µS/cm and applies the ±5 µS/cm / ±3 percent criteria to the check standard but it never states that the standards are potassium chloride solutions traceable to NIST. Unmet: States that potassium chloride solutions traceable to NIST are the standards used

The answer gives the EPA default pH ±0.3 and DO ±0.5 criteria but omits the QA-plan-governs condition and both USGS figures (±0.05 pH ±0.2 mg/L) declining the USGS part as unavailable. Unmet: Defaults apply only when the project QA plan does not specify its own drift criteria; USGS pH practice tighter recalibrate when buffer off by more than ±0.05 pH unit; USGS oxygen verification accepts A6.2 saturation check within ±0.2 mg/L

The answer states daily pre-use calibration and the end-of-day drift check but omits the measurement-mode/standard-reading detail the requirement to qualify out-of-criteria data and the midday-drift qualification limit. Unmet: End-of-day check done in measurement mode not calibration mode by reading one of the standards used that morning; Data falling outside the drift criteria must be qualified; If a midday check finds drift and recalibration succeeds qualification limited to data before that check

The answer makes the manufacturer's position the before-every-field-trip check and the recalibrate-on-failed-check points but it never states verification at the field site and gives the ±5 µS/cm / ±3% limits without the ≤100 µS/cm breakpoint so the acceptance criterion is incomplete. Unmet: States that accuracy must be verified at the field site against a standard before measurements are made; Gives the acceptance criterion as within plus or minus 5 microsiemens per centimetre at or below 100 microsiemens per centimetre or plus or minus 3 percent above that

The answer names ZoBell's solution the reference-potential correction and the ±5 mV pass criterion but omits the 15–30 minute equilibration step and never gives the ~430 mV expected value at 25 °C. Unmet: States the solution and sensors are allowed roughly 15 to 30 minutes to reach the same temperature before reading; States the expected value depends on temperature giving about 430 millivolts at 25 degrees Celsius
All four must-contain points are made correctly and no must-not item is violated.

All four must-contain points are made — the USGS 6.5–8.5 river description is reported as background the pod threshold is stated unavailable and the answer declines to judge 8.7 for the pod — and no must-not is violated since the natural-water comparison is framed as typical background rather than a pod threshold or regulatory limit.

The answer correctly names the calibration slope gives the 95-101 percent range with its 56.2-59.8 mV/pH at 25 °C equivalent and invents no threshold but it omits the one-to-two-minute buffer response-time point and attributes the range to no source. Unmet: Notes that a healthy electrode also responds quickly in buffer on the order of one to two minutes

The answer correctly picks the pH 7 and 10.01 buffers and states the ±10 °C buffer-temperature guidance but it omits the pH-7-first calibration order and never says the temperature-corrected buffer value must be used instead of the nominal value. Unmet: States that calibration begins with the pH 7 buffer when the meter does not dictate an order; States that a buffer's pH value shifts with temperature so the temperature-corrected value must be used rather than the nominal value

The answer correctly flags 92% as below range cleans/recalibrates before replacement reconditions per manufacturer and replaces only if the slope stays below 95% but it omits checking the fill hole and the applicability caveat for the electrode design. Unmet: Checks electrode condition and reference-junction flow; checks filling solution and an open fill hole only when applicable to the electrode design

The answer gives the correct order with temperature first conductivity before pH DO then ORP and the increasing-ionic-strength rationale but omits the point that pH buffers and electrode filling solutions are high in ionic strength and would contaminate a conductivity calibration. Unmet: Notes specifically that pH buffers and electrode filling solutions are high in ionic strength and would contaminate a conductivity calibration

The answer gives the two-solution minimum names standard buffer values and states they must bracket the sample pH but it only mentions NIST traceability and never states buffers must not be past their expiration date. Unmet: Buffers must be NIST-traceable and not past expiration
